title: Optimal competitive ratio for general convex body chasing
short_statement: A recent preprint reports tight linear dimension dependence for general convex body chasing, including Euclidean movement.
open_problem: Verify the reported resolution of the general dimension-only gap; do not conflate it with nested or bounded-horizon chasing.
background: Convex body chasing requires an online point to enter each successive convex body, paying movement in a fixed norm. Dimension-only chaseability was established earlier; the remaining general-versus-nested distinction is essential. The new lower bound below addresses arbitrary nonnested sequences.
full_statement: Starting from $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, an online algorithm receives nonempty convex bodies $K_1,\ldots,K_T$ sequentially and selects $x_t\in K_t$, paying $\sum_t\|x_t-x_{t-1}\|$. The offline optimum minimizes the same cost with the full sequence known. The historical question asks for the optimal dimension-only competitive ratio over arbitrary finite sequences, with no nesting assumption. The new theorem in the What Is Known section reports a matching lower bound for the existing linear upper bound.
known_results: Christianson, 'A Linear Lower Bound for Convex Body Chasing in Every Norm' (arXiv:2610.32670v2, November 3, 2026), Theorem 1, proves a universal $\Omega(d)$ lower bound in every d-dimensional normed space, including Euclidean space and randomized expected cost against fixed input sequences. Combined with Sellke's $O(d)$ upper bound, this reports $\Theta(d)$ worst-case dimension dependence. It does not settle the nested variant or the sharper dependence on a bounded number of requests.

progress.summary: The general dimension-only gap is reported closed by a linear lower bound; full proof not independently checked.

counterexample_rationale: A lower-bound family, not an isolated finite trajectory, is required for dimension-dependent claims.
alphaevolve_rationale: The object of interest is an online algorithm (a strategy over an unbounded, adversarially-revealed sequence of convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^d$) together with an asymptotic competitive-ratio proof, not a fixed finite combinatorial structure; an evolutionary/code-search loop could at best explore small, fixed-$d$, fixed-$N$ instances or heuristics, which would not by itself yield or verify a dimension-general asymptotic bound.

literature.synthesis: The earlier Euclidean lower bound and request-count-dependent upper bounds are historical context. The new result separates the unrestricted sequence model from nested chasing.

reviewed.ref: J. Friedman, N. Linial, 'On convex body chasing', Discrete & Computational Geometry, 1993
reviewed.result: Introduces the problem; proves $\Omega(\sqrt d)$ competitive-ratio lower bound via chasing faces of a hypercube; conjectures a dimension-only competitive ratio exists.

reviewed.ref: S. Bubeck, Y.T. Lee, Y. Li, M. Sellke, 'Competitively Chasing Convex Bodies', STOC 2019 / SIAM J. Comput. 2021
reviewed.result: First finite competitive ratio for general convex body chasing: $2^{O(d)}$, resolving the 1993 chaseability conjecture.

reviewed.ref: D. Argue, S. Gollapudi, G. Guruganesh, A. Schild, 'Chasing Convex Bodies with Linear Competitive Ratio', J. ACM 2021 (SODA 2020)
reviewed.result: Gives an $O(\min(d, \sqrt{d \log T}))$-competitive algorithm for sequences of length $T$, the first linear-in-$d$ bound.

reviewed.ref: M. Sellke, 'Chasing Convex Bodies Optimally', SODA 2020 (arXiv:1905.11968)
reviewed.result: Gives a $d$-competitive algorithm in any normed space (tight for $\ell^\infty$) and $O(\sqrt{d \log N})$-competitive in Euclidean space, via the functional Steiner point of the work function; current best known upper bound for the general problem.

reviewed.ref: N. Bansal, M. Böhm, M. Elias, G. Koumoutsos, S.W. Umboh, 'Nested Convex Bodies are Chaseable', SODA 2018 (arXiv:1707.05527)
reviewed.result: Historical chaseability result for nested convex bodies; not a resolution of the general nonnested model. The previously attributed near-optimal Steiner-point bound is not asserted here.

reviewed.ref: A. Kupavskii, 'The Role of Dimension in the Online Chasing Problem', arXiv:2307.09350, 2023
reviewed.result: Develops a general framework for $\Omega(d^c)$ lower bounds on convex body chasing and shows doubling/Assouad dimension of a metric space do not control chaseability of general ball-chasing.

reviewed.ref: Nicolas Christianson, 'A Linear Lower Bound for Convex Body Chasing in Every Norm' (2026)
reviewed.result: Theorem 1 reports the matching general lower bound.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Audit the lower-bound reduction, randomized quantifiers, and extension from Euclidean to arbitrary norms.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Any claimed improvement to either bound must be checked as a genuine proof, not a numerical experiment: an upper-bound proof must specify the algorithm/potential function and verify the potential-drop or amortized-cost argument holds for arbitrary $d$ and arbitrary (possibly adversarially chosen, unboundedly long) convex-body sequences, not just sampled instances; a lower-bound proof must exhibit an explicit family of convex-body sequences (parametrized by $d$) together with a proof that every online algorithm incurs cost $\Omega(f(d)) \cdot \mathrm{OPT}$ against them. Common failure modes: bounds that secretly depend on $N$ or $T$ being conflated with dimension-only bounds; results that only apply to the nested case being mistakenly cited as resolving the general case; and conflating different published years/venues of the same author's results (e.g., Sellke's 2019 arXiv preprint vs. the 2020 SODA publication) when checking novelty.

where_posed.text: Posed by J. Friedman and N. Linial, 'On convex body chasing', Discrete & Computational Geometry, 1993.
where_posed.location: Original paper (1993); the $\Omega(\sqrt d)$ vs. dimension-only-competitive-ratio question is restated as an explicit open problem in Bubeck, Lee, Li, Sellke, 'Competitively Chasing Convex Bodies', and again in Sellke, 'Chasing Convex Bodies Optimally' (SODA 2020), Section 1.
